steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper on DataInf, an efficient way to estimate data influence in LoRA-tuned LLMs and diffusion models. Motivate why influence of training data matters, explain why the influence function is too costly for large models, and summarize what DataInf does and how we evaluate it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and text-to-image models: strong but still make errors rooted in training data
- Influence function as a framework for training data impact
- Computational cost problem for large models
- DataInf: method, analysis, experiments, code

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Modern large language models (LLMs) and text-to-image models have shown remarkable abilities to generate human-like texts and photorealistic images, and this has led to many real-world applications such as translation, dialogue systems, and image editing. But even state-of-the-art models still generate predictions that are factually incorrect or even biased, and often this is because of problems in the training data. This shows that we need principled and systematic methods to quantify the impact of specific training data points. The influence function gives a rigorous framework to evaluate the impact of each training data point on the predictions of the model. It has been shown to work in various downstream machine learning tasks: mislabeled data detection, best subset selection, model interpretation, and investigating model biases.

The influence function has shown promising results, but using it in real-world scenarios has practical challenges because the computational costs are expensive. To calculate the influence function we need to compute the inverse Hessian matrix, and this needs a lot of computation. Previous studies have tried to reduce this burden, but most of the existing methods still need an iterative algorithm, multiple eigenvalue decompositions or training many models to get accurate influence estimates. Because of this it has been very hard to compute the influence function for large models like LLMs and diffusion models.

- DataInf
  - efficient influence approximation, easy-to-compute closed form
  - better computational + memory complexity than state-of-the-art influence algorithms
  - approximation error analysis: esp. effective for parameter-efficient fine-tuned models
  - experiments: approximation error, mislabeled data detection, influential data identification -> faster, better retrieval
  - RoBERTa, Llama-2-13B-chat, stable-diffusion-v1.5
  - code: https://github.com/ykwon0407/DataInf

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Modern large language models (LLMs) and text-to-image models have shown remarkable abilities to generate human-like texts and photorealistic images, and this has led to many real-world applications such as translation, dialogue systems, and image editing. But even state-of-the-art models still generate predictions that are factually incorrect or even biased, and often this is because of problems in the training data. This shows that we need principled and systematic methods to quantify the impact of specific training data points. The influence function gives a rigorous framework to evaluate the impact of each training data point on the predictions of the model. It has been shown to work in various downstream machine learning tasks: mislabeled data detection, best subset selection, model interpretation, and investigating model biases.

The influence function has shown promising results, but using it in real-world scenarios has practical challenges because the computational costs are expensive. To calculate the influence function we need to compute the inverse Hessian matrix, and this needs a lot of computation. Previous studies have tried to reduce this burden, but most of the existing methods still need an iterative algorithm, multiple eigenvalue decompositions or training many models to get accurate influence estimates. Because of this it has been very hard to compute the influence function for large models like LLMs and diffusion models.

We propose DataInf, an influence approximation method that is computationally efficient and can be easily applied to large-scale machine learning models. DataInf is based on a closed-form expression that is easy to compute, and so it has better computational and memory complexities than the existing state-of-the-art algorithms for computing influence. Our analysis of the approximation error suggests that DataInf is especially effective for parameter-efficient fine-tuned models. We test how well DataInf works in practice with three sets of experiments: approximation error analysis, mislabeled data detection, and influential data identification. The results show that DataInf is faster than existing algorithms and also more effective at retrieving the most (or the least) influential training data points. We apply DataInf to the RoBERTa, Llama-2-13B-chat, and stable-diffusion-v1.5 models, which shows it can be easily applied to LLMs and large diffusion models. Python-based implementation codes are available at https://github.com/ykwon0407/DataInf.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Modern large language models (LLMs) and text-to-image models have demonstrated remarkable abilities in generating human-like texts and photorealistic images, leading to diverse real-world applications such as translation, dialogue systems, and image editing [1,2,3]. Nevertheless, even state-of-the-art models generate factually incorrect or even biased outputs [4,5,6], often as a result of issues in the training data. This highlights the need for principled and systematic methods to quantify the impact of specific training data points. The influence function provides a rigorous framework for evaluating the impact of each training data point on model predictions [7,8], and its efficacy has been demonstrated across various downstream machine learning tasks: mislabeled data detection [9], best subset selection [10,11], model interpretation [12,13,14], and investigation of model biases [15,16].

Despite these promising results, applying the influence function in real-world scenarios poses practical challenges because of its expensive computational cost. Calculating the influence function requires computing the inverse Hessian matrix, which is computationally intensive. Previous studies have attempted to reduce this burden, but most existing methods still require an iterative algorithm [17,18], multiple eigenvalue decompositions [19] or the training of numerous models [10] to obtain accurate influence estimates. It has therefore been very challenging to compute the influence function for large models such as LLMs [20,21,22] and diffusion models [23,24,2].

We propose DataInf, a computationally efficient influence approximation method that can be easily applied to large-scale machine learning models. DataInf is based on an easy-to-compute closed-form expression, which gives it better computational and memory complexities than existing state-of-the-art influence computation algorithms. Our approximation error analysis suggests that DataInf is especially effective for parameter-efficient fine-tuned models. We evaluate the practical efficacy of DataInf through three sets of experiments: approximation error analysis, mislabeled data detection, and influential data identification. Our empirical results show that DataInf is faster than existing algorithms and more effective in retrieving the most (or the least) influential training data points. We apply DataInf to the RoBERTa, Llama-2-13B-chat, and stable-diffusion-v1.5 models, demonstrating that it is easily applicable to LLMs and large-scale diffusion models. Python-based implementation codes are available at https://github.com/ykwon0407/DataInf.
